def:frobenius-dual-h3:
Definition Frobenius dual K^\vee in H_3(q). Let G_{ij} = \mathrm{tr}_M(b_i \cdot b_j) be the Gram matrix of the Frobenius pairing on the NF basis \{b_i\} of H_3(q) (Frobenius Gram matrix), read at z = q^3/(q^2+1) on the quotient H_3/\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{tr}_M \cong \mathrm{TL}_3, where the induced pairing is non-degenerate. For a state K = \sum_i c_i b_i in NF, the Frobenius dual is the unique element K^\vee \in H_3(q) satisfying \langle K^\vee, b_j \rangle_F = c_j for all j. Explicitly:

  K^\vee = \sum_{i,j} c_i (G^{-1})_{ij} b_j.
rem:frobenius-dual-h3-remark:
Remark Degeneracy on H_3 and existence of the Frobenius dual. On H_3 itself the Gram matrix is degenerate: \det G = 0 identically, the (1^3) block being the radical of the Markov trace (MarkovGramDegenerate.lean). Non-degeneracy therefore holds on H_3/\mathrm{rad} \cong \mathrm{TL}_3 and not on H_3.

The dual exists and is unique by non-degeneracy of G on that quotient: the pairing \langle K^\vee, b_j \rangle_F = \sum_{i,k} c_i (G^{-1})_{ik} G_{kj} = \sum_i c_i \delta_{ij} = c_j follows from G^{-1} G = I.

rem:frobenius-gram-matrix-context:
Remark NF Markov-trace computation, operator identification via the dual, and the annihilation identity. The Frobenius self-duality A \cong A^\vee induces a concrete bilinear form on H_3(q) via the Markov trace. The Gram matrix G_{ij} = \mathrm{tr}_M(b_i \cdot b_j) over the NF basis encodes all interaction pairings, and its inverse G^{-1} gives the explicit dual construction K^\vee = \sum_{i,j} c_i (G^{-1})_{ij} b_j.

G is singular on H_3 — read G^{-1} on the Temperley–Lieb quotient. Writing G^{-1} on all of H_3(q) presupposes \det G \neq 0. At the Markov parameter z = q^3/(q^2+1), the relation z(q^2+1) = q^3 forces y_{(1^3)} = 0 identically, so the (1^3) block is the radical of the trace form, \det G = 0 — not "numerically singular", zero — and no inverse exists on H_3(q); at n = 3 the corank is 1.

The Frobenius structure itself is not lost, only relocated: the radical is a two-sided ideal, so \mathrm{tr}_M descends to H_3/\mathrm{rad} \cong \mathrm{TL}_3 and the induced pairing there is non-degenerate. Every use of G^{-1} and of K^\vee below should be read on that 5-dimensional quotient (\sum \dim^2 = C_3 = 5), not on the 6-dimensional H_3.

Proved: a zero-weight block lies in the radical, hence \det G = 0, and the pairing descends to the quotient by the radical.

Markov trace of NF basis elements

Write h = q - q^{-1} and z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1).

See Table 1.

The trace of e^- follows from the Ocneanu--Wenzl Markov recursion (cyclicity + Hecke quadratic + Markov axiom restricted to the sub-algebra): \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0) = \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1\sigma_0^2) \;\text{(cyclicity)} = \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1(h\sigma_0+1)) \;\text{(Hecke quadratic)} = h\cdot\mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1\sigma_0) + \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1) = h \cdot z\,\mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_0) + z = hz^2 + z (the last step uses the Markov axiom on \sigma_1 paired with \sigma_0 \in H_1).

At the proton-pinned q_0 \approx 1.1099785828 with z = q^3/(q^2+1), hz^2 + z \approx 0.6912, and the naive z^3 \approx 0.2300 is off by a factor of 3.0.

Operator identification via the dual

The Frobenius dual (def:frobenius-dual-h3) exactly identifies each basis element with its corresponding knot operator.

Proposition (operator identification). For each NF basis element b_k, the pairing of b_k^\vee with the knot operators \beta(T_{m,n}) satisfies:

See Table 2.

Each basis element pairs maximally with exactly one knot operator (the operator whose braid word contains that element). The electron dual e^{-\vee} pairs with T_{2,3} (trefoil) with coefficient 1 — the Frobenius dual selects the trefoil operator for the electron.

Annihilation identity (symbolic)

Proposition. e^- \cdot e^+ = \gamma (the photon / identity), for all q.
prf:frobenius-gram-matrix:
Proof Proof of frobenius gram matrix. Proof. The braid word \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 \cdot \sigma_0^{-1}\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_0^{-1} = \mathbf{1} by the group law in B_3. No Hecke reduction is needed — the cancellation is exact in the braid group, hence exact in H_3(q) for all q.

Equivalently, this is the Hopf relation (vertex algebra relations, QU-2d): \mu(S \otimes \mathrm{id})\Delta = \eta\varepsilon, where S(\sigma_i) = \sigma_i^{-1} is the antipode. The identity e^- \cdot e^+ = \gamma is the Hopf relation evaluated on the electron word e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 (whose closure is the positive Hopf link T(2,2)).

Witness: the Gram-matrix dual computation.
thm:em-spectral-completeness:
Theorem Two-strand spectral completeness over a commutative ring R. Setup (commutative ring of coefficients). Throughout, the categorical structure is R-enriched over

  R \;=\; \mathbb{Z}\bigl[q^{\pm 1/2},\, (q - q^{-1})^{-1}\bigr].

Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a rigid braided monoidal category R-enriched with self-dual fundamental object A of categorical dimension \dim_q A = [2]_q \in R, and \tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-mod} the fibre functor.

Theorem (two-strand spectral completeness). The Frobenius R-algebra E := \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A \otimes A) is a free R-module of rank 2 with the following structure.

  1. There exist exactly two non-zero central idempotents e_+, e_- \in E with e_+ + e_- = \mathrm{id}_{A \otimes A} and e_+ \cdot e_- = 0.
  2. Each e_\pm projects onto a simple summand: 
      A \otimes A \;\cong\; V_+ \oplus V_-,
  \qquad e_\pm A^{\otimes 2} = V_\pm.
    The summand V_- is canonically isomorphic to the unit object \mathbf{1} — a singlet of R-rank one.
  3. In the unimodular half-power normalisation (c_{A,A} - q^{1/2})(c_{A,A} + q^{-1/2}) = 0, the braiding decomposes as 
      c_{A,A} \;=\; q^{1/2}\, e_+ \;-\; q^{-1/2}\, e_-,
    and \{q^{1/2},\, -q^{-1/2}\} are the only eigenvalues of c_{A,A} on A \otimes A. Equivalently, the rescaled generator \sigma := q^{1/2}\,c_{A,A} = q\,e_+ - q^{-1}\,e_- satisfies the monograph's integer-power Iwahori--Hecke relation \sigma^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma + 1 with eigenvalues \{q,\, -q^{-1}\} and identical central idempotents e_\pm.
  4. (Trace completeness.) With \dim_q V_+ = [3]_q and \dim_q V_- = 1, the normalised categorical traces of the idempotents 
      w_\pm \;:=\; \frac{\mathrm{tr}_q(e_\pm)}{\mathrm{tr}_q(\mathrm{id}_{A \otimes A})}
  \;=\; \frac{\dim_q V_\pm}{[2]_q^{\,2}}
    satisfy w_+ + w_- = 1, because [3]_q + 1 = [2]_q^{\,2}.
prf:em-spectral-completeness:
Proof Proof of em spectral completeness. Proof. The braiding eigenvalue extraction (eigenvalue extraction) shows that c_{A,A} satisfies the Hecke minimal polynomial

  (c_{A,A} - q^{1/2})(c_{A,A} + q^{-1/2}) \;=\; 0

in E. The two eigenvalues q^{1/2}, -q^{-1/2} are distinct (their difference q^{1/2} + q^{-1/2} is a unit in R), so the minimal polynomial splits over R and Bezout produces orthogonal idempotents

  e_- \;=\; \frac{q^{1/2} \cdot \mathrm{id} - c_{A,A}}{q^{1/2} + q^{-1/2}}
      \;=\; \frac{q \cdot \mathrm{id} - \sigma}{q + q^{-1}},
  \qquad
  e_+ \;=\; \mathrm{id} - e_-
      \;=\; \frac{\sigma + q^{-1} \cdot \mathrm{id}}{q + q^{-1}},

where \sigma := q^{1/2}\,c_{A,A} satisfies the integer-power Hecke quadratic (\sigma - q)(\sigma + q^{-1}) = 0, i.e. \sigma^2 = (q - q^{-1})\sigma + 1, over the subring \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}, (q + q^{-1})^{-1}] \subset R. These idempotents are central in E since c_{A,A} (or \sigma) generates the centraliser of the diagonal R-action by Schur--Weyl-Hecke duality. Statement (2) follows from H_2(R, q) \cong E being free of rank 2 over R: E has at most two simple summands, and e_\pm realise them. The singlet identification V_- \cong \mathbf{1} is the standard Schur-functor decomposition A \otimes A = S^2 A \oplus \Lambda^2 A with \Lambda^2 A \cong \mathbf{1} when A is the fundamental of \mathrm{SU}_q(2). Statement (4) follows from (1) and (2): the categorical trace is additive, so \mathrm{tr}_q(e_+) + \mathrm{tr}_q(e_-) = \mathrm{tr}_q(\mathrm{id}_{A \otimes A}) = (\dim_q A)^2 = [2]_q^{\,2}, and \mathrm{tr}_q(e_\pm) = \dim_q V_\pm with \dim_q V_+ = [3]_q, \dim_q V_- = 1. This is the n = 2 case of the Wedderburn trace identity with multiplicities 1. The squared form (\dim_q V_\pm)^2/[2]_q! does not sum to 1: it gives ([3]_q^2 + 1)/[2]_q, which is 5 at q = 1. \square
prop:borromean-markov-trace-closed-form:
Proposition Borromean Markov trace \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = (4 + h^2 - 3h^4 - h^6)/(h^2 + 4). The Markov trace of the Borromean braid \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} = (\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2)^3 on H_3(q), evaluated via the Jones polynomial of the Borromean rings \mathcal{B}_3, admits the exact closed form

  \boxed{\;\;
  \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}, q)
  \;=\;
  \frac{4 + h^2 - 3h^4 - h^6}{h^2 + 4},
  \;\;}

where h = q - q^{-1} and h^2 + 4 = [2]_q^2.

Structural significance for the mass formula

The h^2 = 0 result separates the proton-mass h-dependence into clean layers:

Factor in F_{\mathrm{Bor}} = \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) \cdot [3]_q! / q^3 h^2 coefficient Source
\mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) 0 per-partition cancellation (this proposition)
[3]_q! = (h^2 + 3)\sqrt{h^2 + 4} 11/4 algebraic (q-factorial)
q^3 (denominator) 9/8 algebraic (q = (h + \sqrt{h^2+4})/2)
F_{\mathrm{Bor}} (combined) 19/2 11/4 and 9/8 via division

The exact vanishing of the h^2 term in the trace \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}, q) is an algebraic property of the Borromean rings' Jones polynomial evaluation. In the context of the mass formula, this forces any h^2 dependence in the overall amplitude F_{\mathrm{Bor}} to arise strictly from the normalization factor [3]_q! / q^3.
rem:borromean-colored-jones-habiro-prior:
Remark Prior art: Habiro's coloured Jones formula for the Borromean rings. Habiro computes the Kauffman-bracket invariant of the Borromean rings with each component coloured by an element of the skein module of the solid torus. In the natural basis \{e_n\}, where e_n corresponds to the (n+1)-dimensional irreducible representation of U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2), the value \langle e_l, e_m, e_n\rangle is a finite sum over 0 \le i \le \min(l,m,n) of powers of (a - a^{-1}) times ratios of quantum factorials, symmetric in l, m, n [habiro2000, \S 3, p. 37]. In his modified basis \{R'_n\} the same invariant is diagonal: it is (a - a^{-1})^n\,[2n+1]!/[n]! when l = m = n and 0 otherwise [habiro2000, Prop. 7.1, p. 41].

The closed form of the Borromean Markov trace is the uncoloured case, so this is the published all-colours version of the same invariant, and Prop. 7.1 is a precise locator for the corpus's citations of this key. The paper works in the Kauffman variable a and its own normalisation; it does not compute the Markov trace in H_3(q), so matching the two at the fundamental colour needs the change of variables and framing to be checked first.
prf:borromean-markov-trace-closed-form:
Proof Proof of borromean markov trace closed form. The Jones polynomial of the Borromean rings is [murasugi1996]:

  V(\mathcal{B}_3, t)
  = -t^{-3} + 3t^{-2} - 2t^{-1} + 4 - 2t + 3t^2 - t^3.

Setting t = q^2 and introducing u := q^2 + q^{-2}, this becomes a polynomial in u:

  V = -u^3 + 3u^2 + u - 2.

For a 3-component link, the Markov trace is \mathrm{tr}_M = V / [2]_q^2 where [2]_q^2 = (q + q^{-1})^2 = u + 2. Polynomial long division yields:

  \frac{V}{u + 2}
  = -u^2 + 5u - 9 + \frac{16}{u + 2}.

Substituting u = h^2 + 2 (where h = q - q^{-1}, so q^2 + q^{-2} = h^2 + 2):

  \mathrm{tr}_M
  = -(h^2 + 2)^2 + 5(h^2 + 2) - 9 + \frac{16}{h^2 + 4}
  = \frac{4 + h^2 - 3h^4 - h^6}{h^2 + 4}.

\square

The h-expansion (purely even)

Taylor-expanding around h = 0:

  \mathrm{tr}_M
  = 1
    + \underbrace{0}_{\text{no } h^2}
    \cdot h^2
    - \underbrace{\frac{3}{4}}_{h^4} \cdot h^4
    - \underbrace{\frac{1}{16}}_{h^6} \cdot h^6
    + \underbrace{\frac{1}{64}}_{h^8} \cdot h^8
    + \cdots

The series is purely even in h (the numerator and denominator are both even polynomials in h). The higher-order coefficients follow a geometric tail from the remainder term 16/(h^2 + 4).

The h^2 coefficient is exactly zero

The vanishing of the h^2 term is a non-trivial cancellation: the numerator HAS an h^2 coefficient (+1), but the denominator's h^2 coefficient (+1) cancels it exactly:

  \frac{4 + h^2 - 3h^4 - h^6}{4 + h^2}
  = \frac{(4 + h^2) + (-3h^4 - h^6)}{4 + h^2}
  = 1 + \frac{-3h^4 - h^6}{h^2 + 4}.

The first non-trivial correction appears at h^4 with coefficient -3/4: the first topological invariant of the Borromean linking structure — the part of the Jones polynomial that distinguishes \mathcal{B}_3 from the trivial 3-component unlink.

Per-representation decomposition and exact h^2 budget

The three irreps of S_3 / H_3(q) contribute distinctly to the Frobenius expansion \mathrm{tr}_M = \sum_\lambda y_\lambda \chi^\lambda.

Convention note. Two distinct Markov-trace normalisations are in use for H_3(q), and they have different Wenzl weights and different per-partition budgets:

  1. the Jones-closure normalisation \mathrm{tr}_M = V_{\mathrm{Jones}} / [2]_q^{\,c-1} — the convention of the closed form above — with weights y_{(3)} = [4]_q/[2]_q^3, y_{(2,1)} = 1/[2]_q^2, y_{(1^3)} = 0 identically (Closed-form Jones/Temperley–Lieb weights on H_3(q) (Borromean Jones polynomial));
  2. the Wenzl-bridge / Ocneanu normalisation (used by the formal derivation), whose weights are all non-zero and whose trace value on \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} differs from the closed form above (e.g. 0.91926 vs 0.93917 at q = 1.3; that witness records lean_form_matches: false).

An earlier revision of this section tabulated the bridge-convention budget (5/128, -20/128, 15/128) without labelling the convention — those numbers decompose the bridge trace, not the closed form above. Both budgets sum to zero (each trace separately has h^2 = 0), which masked the mismatch.

In the Jones-closure convention used here, the per-partition decomposition is:

  • \lambda = (3) [trivial, dim 1]: \chi^{(3)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = 1 exactly for all q (writhe-zero braid, trivial eigenvalue q^0 = 1); weight y_{(3)} = [4]_q/[2]_q^3. Per-partition h^2 coefficient of y_{(3)} \cdot \chi^{(3)}: \;+1/8.

  • \lambda = (1^3) [sign, dim 1]: \chi^{(1^3)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = 1 exactly (writhe-zero, sign eigenvalue (-q^{-1})^0 = 1); weight y_{(1^3)} = 0 identically — the Jones polynomial factors through Temperley–Lieb, which annihilates the 3-row partition. Per-partition h^2 coefficient: \;0.

  • \lambda = (2,1) [standard, dim 2]: The only non-abelian irrep, with exact rational character

      \chi^{(2,1)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}})
  = \frac{-q^{12} + 3q^{10} - 3q^8 + 4q^6 - 3q^4 + 3q^2 - 1}{q^6}
  \;=\; 2 - 3h^4 - h^6;

    weight y_{(2,1)} = 1/[2]_q^2. ALL correction terms (h^4, h^6, \ldots) of \mathrm{tr}_M originate from this partition alone. Per-partition h^2 coefficient of y_{(2,1)} \cdot \chi^{(2,1)}: \;-1/8.

The h^2 budget is exact:

  \underbrace{\frac{1}{8}}_{(3)}
  \;+\; \underbrace{\left(-\frac{1}{8}\right)}_{(2,1)}
  \;+\; \underbrace{0}_{(1^3)}
  \;=\; 0.

(For the record, the bridge-convention budget is (5/128, -20/128, 15/128), also summing to zero — but it decomposes the bridge-normalised trace, a different functional.)

Vanishing of h^2: universal identity + Borromean symmetry

The cancellation follows from two independent facts:

Fact 1 (universal). The Markov trace normalization \sum_\lambda y_\lambda(q) \cdot d_\lambda = 1 holds identically in q. Differentiating twice in h at h = 0:

  \sum_\lambda \bigl[h^2\text{-coeff of } y_\lambda\bigr] \cdot d_\lambda = 0.

This is a knot-independent identity — it constrains the Wenzl weights regardless of which braid is traced.

Fact 2 (Borromean-specific). The braid \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} = (\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2)^3 maps under \pi\colon B_3 \to S_3 to (s_1 s_2)^3 = (1\,2\,3)^3 = \mathrm{id}. Since it also has writhe = 3 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot (-1) = 0, the one-dimensional characters satisfy \chi^{(3)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = \chi^{(1^3)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = 1 exactly. At q = 1 (i.e. h = 0), the standard character evaluates to \chi^{(2,1)}(\mathrm{id}) = d_{(2,1)} = 2.

Fact 3 (Borromean-specific). The standard character has no h^2 term: \chi^{(2,1)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = 2 - 3h^4 - h^6.

Combining: write \mathrm{tr}_M = \sum_\lambda y_\lambda \chi^\lambda and take the h^2 coefficient. It is

  \sum_\lambda \bigl[h^2\bigr] y_\lambda \cdot \chi^\lambda\big|_{h=0}
  \;+\; \sum_\lambda y_\lambda\big|_{h=0} \cdot \bigl[h^2\bigr] \chi^\lambda .

The first sum is \sum_\lambda [h^2]y_\lambda \cdot d_\lambda = 0 by Facts 1 and 2. In the second sum the one-dimensional characters are constant, so only y_{(2,1)}|_{h=0} \cdot [h^2]\chi^{(2,1)} survives, and it vanishes by Fact 3.

Generalization: conditions for h^2 = 0

The argument needs three conditions on \beta \in B_n:

  1. Pure braid: \pi(\beta) = \mathrm{id} \in S_n (so \chi^\lambda(\beta)|_{q=1} = d_\lambda for all \lambda).
  2. Writhe zero: equal positive and negative crossings (so 1-dimensional characters are identically 1).
  3. No h^2 term in the multi-dimensional characters: [h^2]\chi^\lambda(\beta) = 0 for every \lambda with y_\lambda|_{h=0} \neq 0 and d_\lambda > 1.

Conditions 1 and 2 alone do not suffice, even at H_3. The pure, writhe-zero braid \sigma_1^2 \sigma_2^{-2} has \chi^{(2,1)} = 2 + 3h^2 + h^4 and \mathrm{tr}_M = 1 + \tfrac34 h^2 + O(h^4) at z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1).

Cross-isotope verification: the deuteron (H_6), tritium (H_9), and {}^3\mathrm{He} (H_9) atom braids have h^2 \ne 0 (12.7, 18.7, 36.6 respectively). The three conditions are sufficient for every n, so each of these braids violates at least one of them.
prop:borromean-two-photon-factorisation:
Proposition The Borromean braid is a product of two commuting photons in H_3(q). Let A be an algebra over a commutative ring, and let \sigma_0, \sigma_1 \in A satisfy the relations of H_3(q): \sigma_i^2 = h\,\sigma_i + 1 and \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 = \sigma_1\sigma_0\sigma_1, where h = q - q^{-1}. Put V = \sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1} = \sigma_0\sigma_1 - h\,\sigma_0. Then

  V^3 = 1 + h^2 V - h^2 V^2,
  \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
  (V - 1)\bigl(V^2 + (1 + h^2)V + 1\bigr) = 0,

and

  (\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1})^3 = (1 + q h V)\,(1 - q^{-1} h V).

Each factor is a photon \gamma(\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \varphi_{01}) = 1 + \varphi_0\sigma_0 + \varphi_1\sigma_1 + \varphi_{01}\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1} that carries only its vertex term:

  1 + q h V = \gamma(0,\, 0,\, q h),
  \qquad
  1 - q^{-1} h V = \gamma(0,\, 0,\, -q^{-1} h),

so (\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1})^3 = \gamma(0,0,qh)\,\gamma(0,0,-q^{-1}h). In the normal-form basis these are 1 - q h^2\,\sigma_0 + q h\,\sigma_0\sigma_1 and 1 + q^{-1} h^2\,\sigma_0 - q^{-1} h\,\sigma_0\sigma_1.

The two factors commute.

Proof. In the right-associated words of \sigma_0, \sigma_1, rewrite \sigma_0\sigma_0 \mapsto h\sigma_0 + 1, \sigma_1\sigma_1 \mapsto h\sigma_1 + 1 and \sigma_1\sigma_0\sigma_1 \mapsto \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0. This gives

  V^2 = \sigma_1\sigma_0 - h^2\,\sigma_0\sigma_1 - h\,\sigma_1 + h^3\,\sigma_0 + h^2,
  V^3 = -h^2\,\sigma_1\sigma_0 + h^3\,\sigma_1 + (1 - h^4) + (h^4 + h^2)\,\sigma_0\sigma_1 - (h^5 + h^3)\,\sigma_0 ,

and comparing the two gives the cubic relation. The product of the two factors is 1 + (q - q^{-1}) h V - h^2 V^2 = 1 + h^2 V - h^2 V^2. The factors are polynomials in V, so they commute. \square

The statement and its proof hold in every algebra that satisfies the relations, so it holds in H_3(q) itself and in each of its representations. It uses no division, no ordering and no value of q.

Relation to the braid used for \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}). In the closed-form proposition the braid is written (\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2)^3 with generators numbered from 1. Relabelled to \sigma_0, \sigma_1, that is (\sigma_0^{-1}\sigma_1)^3. The flip \sigma_0 \leftrightarrow \sigma_1 (conjugation by the half twist) sends it to (\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_0)^3 = \sigma_1^{-1}(\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1})^3\sigma_1. So the two braids are conjugate and have the same Markov trace. The identity above is for (\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1})^3.

Scope. The identity says that \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}, read as a Hecke element, is a product of two photons, each reduced to its vertex term, with weights set by the two eigenvalues q and -q^{-1} of \sigma_i. It does not select \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}: products of two such photons reach almost every element of H_3(q). It changes no number. Because the two factors commute, the order of the photons cannot distinguish the proton from the neutron.
prop:trace-flavour-no-go:
Proposition A cyclic trace on H_3(q) cannot separate a nucleon word from its flip–reversal. Let A be an algebra over a commutative ring R generated by \sigma_0, \sigma_1 subject to the relations of H_3(q), with h = q - q^{-1}. Let t : A \to R be R-linear with t(xy) = t(yx). Let \theta be the anti-automorphism that exchanges \sigma_0 \leftrightarrow \sigma_1 and reverses products. For every product x = f_1 \cdots f_m of factors f_k = \alpha_k + \beta_k \sigma_{i_k},

  t(\theta(x)) = t(x).

The factors include \sigma_i^{-1} = \sigma_i - h, every typed crossing operator C(f, f'; \sigma_i) of the typed crossing operator, and their inverses. A Markov trace is such a t.

Proof. The exchange is inner. With \Delta = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0, the braid relation gives \Delta\sigma_0 = \sigma_1\Delta and \Delta\sigma_1 = \sigma_0\Delta, and \Delta is invertible with inverse \sigma_0^{-1}\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_0^{-1}. So t of the exchanged product equals t(\Delta x \Delta^{-1}) = t(x).

For reversal, every product of factors reduces to a combination of the six elements 1, \sigma_0, \sigma_1, \sigma_0\sigma_1, \sigma_1\sigma_0, \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0. The relations \sigma_i^2 = h\sigma_i + 1 and \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 = \sigma_1\sigma_0\sigma_1 read the same backwards. Multiplying on the right in the original order and on the left in the reversed order therefore produces the same coefficients, with \sigma_0\sigma_1 and \sigma_1\sigma_0 exchanged. A cyclic trace gives t(\sigma_0\sigma_1) = t(\sigma_1\sigma_0). \square

Consequence. Every typed nucleon word whose flavour assignment is carried to another one by \theta has the same trace as that word. In particular this holds for the six placements of the odd quark on (\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1})^3. A difference between proton and neutron therefore requires an ingredient that is not a cyclic trace of such a product.

  • the photon \gamma(\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \varphi_{01}) = 1 + \varphi_0\sigma_0 + \varphi_1\sigma_1 + \varphi_{01}\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1} equals 1 + (\varphi_0 - h\varphi_{01})\sigma_0 + \varphi_1\sigma_1 + \varphi_{01}\sigma_0\sigma_1, so the earlier form with last term \sigma_0\sigma_1 is the same family of elements in other coordinates, and the two factors of the two-photon factorisation are photons with only their last term;
  • commuting separators can be moved past a photon;
  • on a 2 \times 2 representation in which \sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1} has no fixed vector and is not a scalar, its trace is -(1 + h^2) and its determinant is 1.
prop:h3-markov-wenzl-weights:

  \boxed{\;\;
  y_{(3)}(q) \;=\; \frac{[4]_q}{[2]_q^{3}},
  \qquad
  y_{(2,1)}(q) \;=\; \frac{1}{[2]_q^{2}},
  \qquad
  y_{(1^3)}(q) \;=\; 0.
  \;\;}

At the symmetric point q = 1 these evaluate to

  \bigl(y_{(3)},\, y_{(2,1)},\, y_{(1^3)}\bigr)\big|_{q=1}
  \;=\;

  \qquad \text{— \emph{not} uniform.}

The scope of this trace normalisation, the immediate Borromean corollary, the chirality of the weights, the notation distinctions, and the significance for the Borromean derivation are collected in the Wenzl-weights context.

prf:h3-markov-wenzl-weights:
Proof Proof of h3 markov wenzl weights. Three steps, each forced.

Step 1 — y_{(1^3)} \equiv 0 (Temperley–Lieb quotient). The Jones polynomial factors through the Temperley–Lieb algebra \mathrm{TL}_n(q) (Kauffman bracket), which is the quotient of \mathrm{H}_n(q) annihilating every V_\lambda with more than two rows. For n = 3 the only such partition is (1^3), so the Jones-normalised Markov trace assigns it weight zero identically in q. Equivalently, the vanishing is the algebraic identity

  [2]_q^{3} - 2\,[2]_q - [4]_q \;=\; 0,

verified by direct expansion: with [2]_q = q + q^{-1}, [2]_q^3 = q^3 + 3q + 3q^{-1} + q^{-3}, so [2]_q^3 - 2[2]_q = q^3 + q + q^{-1} + q^{-3} = [4]_q.

Step 2 — Markov normalisation. \mathrm{tr}_M(\mathbf{1}_3) = 1 (the identity braid closes to the 3-component unlink, whose Jones value is exactly the normalising [2]_q^2). With d_{(3)}, d_{(2,1)}, d_{(1^3)} = 1, 2, 1 and Step 1:

  y_{(3)}(q) + 2\, y_{(2,1)}(q) \;=\; 1.

Step 3 — uniqueness from the Borromean closed form. For \beta_{\mathrm{Bor}} (writhe 0, image \mathrm{id} \in S_3), \chi^{(3)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = 1 exactly and \chi^{(2,1)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = 2 - 3h^4 - h^6 with h = q - q^{-1}. Substituting Steps 1–2:

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}})
  \;=\;
  1 + y_{(2,1)}(q)\,\bigl(\chi^{(2,1)}(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) - 2\bigr)
  \;=\;
  1 - y_{(2,1)}(q)\,\bigl(3h^4 + h^6\bigr).

Comparing with the closed form \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_{\mathrm{Bor}}) = (4 + h^2 - 3h^4 - h^6)/(h^2+4) = 1 - (3h^4 + h^6)/(h^2 + 4), and noting 3h^4 + h^6 \neq 0 for h \neq 0:

  y_{(2,1)}(q) \;=\; \frac{1}{h^2 + 4} \;=\; \frac{1}{[2]_q^{2}}
  \qquad\text{(uniquely, for all } q \neq 1\text{; at } q = 1 \text{ by continuity)}.

Then Step 2 gives y_{(3)} = 1 - 2/[2]_q^2 = ([2]_q^2 - 2)/[2]_q^2 = [4]_q / [2]_q^3 using Step 1's identity. \square

Direction of the argument. Step 3 determines y_{(2,1)} from the Borromean closed form, which already uses the Jones–Temperley–Lieb parameter z = q^3/(q^2+1). The step is therefore an internal consistency computation at z = q^3/(q^2+1) rather than an independent selection of z over other members of the Ocneanu trace family — reading it as a selection argument would be circular. The independent characterisation of z = q^3/(q^2+1) is the Temperley–Lieb uniqueness argument (y_{(1^3)}(z) = 0 has the unique non-trivial root z = q^3/(q^2+1)), whose premise — that the relevant fibre functor lands in \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)) \simeq \mathrm{TL}_3 — is a separate question.
lem:feynman-eigenbasis-decomposition:
Lemma Eigenbasis decomposition for the Feynman amplitude. Let V be the fundamental representation of \mathrm{SU}_q(2) with q not a root of unity. Let \beta \in B_n act on V^{\otimes n} via the braid group representation \rho_n \colon B_n \to \mathrm{Aut}(V^{\otimes n}). Then

  V^{\otimes n}
  \cong
  \bigoplus_{\substack{\lambda \vdash n \\ \ell(\lambda) \leq 2}}
  V_\lambda \otimes S_\lambda,

where V_\lambda is the irreducible \mathrm{SU}_q(2)-module of spin j = (\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)/2 and S_\lambda is the irreducible H_n(R, q)-module. The braid \beta acts on each S_\lambda via the quotient map B_n \to H_n(R, q). The number of summands is \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1, which is finite for every n.

prop:convention-d-kills-antisymmetriser:
Proposition z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1) is the unique non-trivial Markov trace on H_3(q) whose radical contains the three-strand antisymmetriser. Let

  \mathrm{tr}_M \;=\; y_{(3)}\,\chi^{(3)} \;+\; y_{(2,1)}\,\chi^{(2,1)} \;+\; y_{(1^3)}\,\chi^{(1^3)}

be the Wedderburn expansion of a Markov trace on H_3(q), normalised by \mathrm{tr}_M(1) = 1, \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma) = z and \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_0\sigma_1) = z^2. Then for every q > 0

  \boxed{\;\;
  y_{(1^3)} \;=\; 0
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  z \;=\; q
  \;\;\text{ or }\;\;
  z \;=\; \frac{q^{3}}{q^{2}+1},
  \;\;}

and the first root forces y_{(3)} = 1, y_{(2,1)} = y_{(1^3)} = 0. The parameter z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1) therefore defines the unique non-trivial Markov trace on H_3(q) whose radical contains the three-strand antisymmetriser.

Three normalisations, three unknowns

A Markov trace on H_3(q) is determined by its values on three conjugacy classes, and the Wedderburn expansion turns those values into a linear system in the weights. With r a formal inverse for q and the Hoefsmit character values \chi(1) = (1,2,1), \chi(\sigma) = (q,\; q-r,\; -r), \chi(\sigma_0\sigma_1) = (q^{2},\, -1,\, r^{2}), the three normalisations read

\[
\begin{aligned}
  y_{(3)} + 2y_{(2,1)} + y_{(1^3)} &= 1, \\
  q\,y_{(3)} + (q-r)\,y_{(2,1)} - r\,y_{(1^3)} &= z, \\
  q^{2}y_{(3)} - y_{(2,1)} + r^{2}y_{(1^3)} &= z^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Eliminating y_{(3)} and y_{(2,1)} and clearing inverses with qr = 1 leaves the antisymmetric weight in factored form,

  y_{(1^3)}\,(q^{2}+1)(q^{4}+q^{2}+1)
  \;=\;
  q^{2}\,(z - q)\,\bigl(z(q^{2}+1) - q^{3}\bigr).

The scale factor on the left is a sum of even powers and is strictly positive, so it cancels: the antisymmetriser dies at exactly the two roots of the right-hand side, and nowhere else.

The trivial branch is not a competitor

At z = q the whole trace collapses. Substituting the root back into the linear system gives y_{(2,1)} = 0 alongside y_{(1^3)} = 0, hence y_{(3)} = 1: the trace is the one-dimensional character. Such a trace carries no mixed-symmetry block, so the two isospin weights degenerate to 1 and 0 and no nucleon-pair structure survives. It is a Markov trace only in the empty sense, which is what "non-trivial" excludes in the statement above.

The second root is z\,(q^{2}+1) = q^{3}, i.e. z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1). Reading the closed forms off the same system recovers, now derived rather than tabulated,

  y_{(2,1)} \;=\; \frac{q^{2}}{(q^{2}+1)^{2}} \;=\; \frac{1}{[2]_q^{2}},
  \qquad
  y_{(3)} \;=\; \frac{q^{4}+1}{(q^{2}+1)^{2}} \;=\; \frac{[4]_q}{[2]_q^{3}},

the n = 3 instance of the two-row closed form y_{(n-k,k)} = [n-2k+1]_q/[2]_q^{\,n}.

What the characterisation replaces

The selection criterion for the Markov trace is not non-degeneracy. The trace at z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1) violates non-degeneracy by construction --- the pairing has a radical, and the radical is exactly the block killed above --- so a non-degeneracy criterion could never have selected it. What this proposition supplies in its place is a derivation: impose the row cap y_\lambda = 0 for \ell(\lambda) \ge 3 together with faithfulness on the two-row blocks, and z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1) is forced uniquely.

The pinning first becomes available at three strands. On H_2(q) there is no three-row partition whose weight can be asked to vanish, the algebra is commutative with a single generator, and every z is admissible. The row cap is vacuous at n \le 2 and bites at n = 3.

prf:convention-d-kills-antisymmetriser:
Proof Proof: elimination, factorisation, and the exclusion of the trivial branch.

Elimination

The three normalisations are linear in the weights, so the antisymmetric weight is obtained by a single cofactor combination. Multiplying the identity normalisation by (q^{3} - q^{2}r + q), the generator normalisation by -(2q^{2}+1), and the two-crossing normalisation by (q+r), and adding, eliminates y_{(3)} and y_{(2,1)} simultaneously:

  y_{(1^3)}\,\bigl((q^{2}+1+r^{2})(q+r)\bigr)
  \;=\;
  (z^{2}-q^{2})(q+r) \;+\; (2q^{2}+1)(q-z).

No relation between q and r is used, so the identity holds in the polynomial ring before any inverse structure is imposed --- which is what makes it safe to reuse over a coefficient ring where q is not invertible.

Factorisation

Scaling by q^{3} and substituting qr = 1 clears every inverse and exhibits the two roots:

  y_{(1^3)}\,(q^{2}+1)(q^{4}+q^{2}+1)
  \;=\;
  q^{2}\,(z-q)\,\bigl(z(q^{2}+1)-q^{3}\bigr).

Both factors of the scale are sums of even powers with positive coefficients, so the product is strictly positive for every q in an ordered field and may be cancelled. Setting y_{(1^3)} = 0 therefore forces q^{2}(z-q)(z(q^{2}+1)-q^{3}) = 0, and q > 0 removes the factor q^{2}. The two remaining factors give the two roots.

The converse direction is the same identity read the other way: substituting either root annihilates the right-hand side, hence y_{(1^3)} = 0.

Excluding z = q

Only the second root survives, and the argument is that the first carries no algebra. Substituting z = q into the factorisation gives y_{(1^3)} = 0; feeding that back into the generator and two-crossing normalisations leaves a two-by-two system whose solution is y_{(2,1)} = 0, y_{(3)} = 1. The trace is then the one-dimensional character T_w \mapsto q^{\ell(w)}.

Two consequences make the exclusion structural rather than aesthetic. The mixed-symmetry block carries the entire two-dimensional irrep of H_3(q), so a trace with y_{(2,1)} = 0 sees none of it; and the isospin weights, being branch sums over the Bratteli diagram, degenerate to \mu_+ = 1 and \mu_- = 0. A trace that assigns weight zero to one of the two nucleon-pair channels cannot separate them, so the whole selection question it was meant to answer disappears with it.

What remains is the single root z(q^{2}+1) = q^{3}, i.e. z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1).
prop:markov-branching-three-term:
Proposition Branching coherence of the Markov trace reduces to [m+2]_q + [m]_q = [2]_q\,[m+1]_q. Let y_{(n-k,k)} = [n-2k+1]_q/[2]_q^{\,n} be the two-row Markov weights at z = q^3/(q^2+1). Then adding a box to a two-row Young diagram is coherent with the trace,

  y_{(n+1-k,\,k)} \;+\; y_{(n-k,\,k+1)} \;=\; y_{(n-k,\,k)},

and this identity is, after clearing [2]_q^{\,n+1}, exactly the three-term recursion

  \boxed{\;\; [m+2]_q \;+\; [m]_q \;=\; [2]_q\,[m+1]_q. \;\;}

One identity, every level of the tower

The Bratteli diagram of the tower H_2(q) \subset H_3(q) \subset \cdots branches a two-row shape \lambda = (n-k,k) into the two shapes obtained by adding a box to the first or the second row. Coherence of a trace with the inclusion means the parent weight is the sum of the two child weights, which for the closed form above is the recursion displayed. With m = n - 2k + 1 the correspondence is exact: the two children carry [m+2]_q and [m]_q, the parent carries [2]_q\,[m+1]_q, and the common denominator [2]_q^{\,n+1} divides out.

The recursion itself has no content beyond the definition of a q-integer. Writing [m]_q = (q^{m}-q^{-m})/(q-q^{-1}) and abstracting X = q^{m}, Y = q^{-m}, the numerators of [m+2]_q, [m]_q and [m+1]_q are Xq^{2} - Yq^{-2}, X - Y and Xq - Yq^{-1}; the denominator q - q^{-1} is common and cancels, leaving a polynomial identity in the ideal generated by q\,q^{-1} = 1. There is no natural subtraction, no division, and no appeal to SU(2).

One hypothesis is genuinely needed rather than defensive: [2]_q \ne 0. Over an ordered field q\,q^{-1} = 1 and q + q^{-1} = 0 are incompatible, and at the aether parameter [2]_q \ge 2; over \mathbb{C}, however, q^{2} = -1 makes the statement false. The recursion is therefore an identity of the real tower, and the qualification travels with it.

What it buys

Three facts the framework uses separately are the same fact.

  • The isospin weights are branch sums. Restricting from H_3(q) to H_2(q), the totally symmetric and mixed-symmetry blocks both reach the symmetric block of H_2(q), and the mixed-symmetry and antisymmetric blocks both reach the antisymmetric one. That is \mu_+ = y_{(3)} + y_{(2,1)} and \mu_- = y_{(2,1)} + y_{(1^3)}, the n = 3 instance.
  • The next level closes the same way, y_{(3)}[H_3] = y_{(4)} + y_{(3,1)} and y_{(2,1)}[H_3] = y_{(3,1)} + y_{(2,2)}, which are the instances at m = 3 and m = 1.
  • The normalisation \mathrm{tr}_M(1) = 1 is the recursion summed over a level: [2]_q^{\,3} = [4]_q + 2[2]_q at three strands and [2]_q^{\,4} = [5]_q + 3[3]_q + 2[1]_q at four, the multiplicities being the Specht dimensions of the surviving shapes.

Nothing in the list is an independent assumption about the trace. Each is the three-term recursion evaluated at a different m, which is why the tower admits a coherent Markov trace at all.
rem:hecke-radical-is-temperley-lieb:
Remark The radical is the Temperley--Lieb ideal: \sum \dim^{2} over the surviving blocks is C_n. The Markov trace at z = q^3/(q^2+1) does not annihilate the three-strand antisymmetriser by accident. The row cap propagates up the whole tower, and what it leaves behind is a named algebra.

Because the fundamental representation of SU(2) is two-dimensional, no q-antisymmetriser exists on three of its strands, and the Wedderburn weight of any partition with three or more rows vanishes identically --- not numerically at q_0, but as a rational function of q. The surviving blocks of H_n(q) are therefore exactly the two-row shapes. Summing the squared Specht dimensions over those shapes gives, level by level, the Catalan numbers:

n surviving shapes \sum \dim^{2} \dim H_n(q) C_n
2 (2),\,(1,1) 2 2 2
3 (3),\,(2,1) 5 6 5
4 (4),\,(3,1),\,(2,2) 14 24 14
5 (5),\,(4,1),\,(3,2) 42 120 42
6 (6),\,(5,1),\,(4,2),\,(3,3) 132 720 132
7 (7),\,(6,1),\,(5,2),\,(4,3) 429 5040 429

The quotient of H_n(q) by the radical of its Markov form thus has the dimension of the Temperley--Lieb algebra TL_n(q), and the blocks match shape by shape. At n = 4 the bookkeeping closes exactly: 24 - 14 = 10 = 3^{2} + 1^{2}, the discarded (2,1,1) and (1^{4}) blocks, so the quotient is the direct sum of the three surviving matrix algebras and not a proper quotient of it.

Why the quotient is not an amputation

The metric obstruction below asks for a quotient by the radical, and taken on its own that reads as an ad hoc repair. It is not. The radical is the Temperley--Lieb ideal, generated by the three-strand q-antisymmetriser, and the quotient is a well-studied algebra with a diagrammatic calculus and a standard bilinear form. "Quotient by the radical" and "work in TL_n(q)" are one instruction.

Stated the other way: the degeneracy is not an accidental defect of the parameter z = q^3/(q^2+1), it is what the two-row Schur--Weyl quotient means: the Markov trace factors through Temperley--Lieb throughout.

Lineage of the trace-radical quotient

The algebraic ingredients assemble a well-documented lineage. Harold Neville Vazeille Temperley and Elliott H. Lieb [temperley-lieb1971] introduced the planar diagram algebra TL_n of Catalan dimension C_n; Vaughan F. R. Jones [jones1987] and Hans Wenzl [wenzl1988] identified TL_n(q) as the two-row GNS quotient of H_n(q) via explicit Gram determinants and minimal idempotents; and Rosa C. Orellana [orellana1998] together with Meinolf Geck and Sofia Lambropoulou [geck-lambropoulou-2004] gave closed Young-diagram weight formulas characterizing weight-vanishing Markov trace radicals across Iwahori--Hecke towers. Categorically, quotienting by pairings that vanish under every trace closure matches the universal skein construction of Christian Blanchet, Nathan Habegger, Gregor Masbaum, and Pierre Vogel [bhmv1995], Vladimir G. Turaev [turaev2010], and the negligible-morphism ideal of John W. Barrett and Bruce W. Westbury [barrett1993]. What distinguishes the present regime from root-of-unity topological field theory is the parameter locus: skein semisimplification specialises q = e^{i\pi/r} to kill tilting modules of zero quantum dimension, whereas here q > 1 is real and U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2) is semisimple, with the radical generated at every real q by Michio Jimbo's two-row \mathrm{SU}_q(2) Schur--Weyl rank cap [jimbo1986].

What is measured and what is proved

The dimension count above was a measurement rather than a theorem of this paper; it is now a theorem, at every n (below). The measurement came first and is kept, because it is what the theorem was checked against. The weights were evaluated for every partition of n = 2,\dots,7 at 50 decimal places, with worst residual 1.34 \times 10^{-51} against the closed form y_{(n-k,k)} = [n-2k+1]_q/[2]_q^{\,n}. That run is now recorded, and strengthened, in the two-row weight-family computation: rather than a residual at one q, the normalisation is checked as an exact identity in q,

  \sum_{k} f^{(n-k,k)}\,[n-2k+1]_q \;=\; [2]_q^{\,n},

which simplifies symbolically to exactly 0 for n = 2,\dots,10 — so the closed form is a normalised weight family for every q at once, which no finite-precision evaluation can establish. The Specht dimensions are cross-checked by two independent routes (ballot and hook-length), and the table above is reproduced rather than cited.

What is now proved, at general n. Four statements, none of which is the isomorphism:

  • \sum_\lambda \dim_\lambda\, y_\lambda = 1 --- the normalisation \mathrm{tr}(1) = 1;
  • \sum_k m_k(n)\,[n{+}1{-}2k]_q = [2]_q^{\,n} --- the same identity with the denominator cleared, i.e. the q-dimension count of V^{\otimes n};
  • \sum \dim^2 = C_n over the two-row shapes and, separately, over the two-column shapes;
  • \dim \lambda = \dim \lambda' for this family, which the next section had been asserting without backing.

The isomorphism and the ideal equality are now proved (the theorem). Over any field of characteristic zero and for q \neq 0 not a root of unity, H_n(q)/\mathrm{rad} \cong TL_n(q + q^{-1}) as algebras, with e_i \mapsto q - \sigma_i; the proof compares the Catalan dimension count above with a Jones normal-form spanning set of TL_n, so the counts are an ingredient of the proof and not a substitute for it. At the level of ideals, the kernel of the quotient map H_n(q) \to TL_n in the presentation U_i = T_i + 1 equals \theta(\mathrm{rad}), where \theta \colon \sigma_i \mapsto -\sigma_i^{-1} is the involution exchanging the two eigenvalues q and -q^{-1}. Without \theta the inclusion fails already at three strands: on the one-row block (3) the relator acts by (q^2+1)(q^4+q^2+1) \neq 0. The trace radical is a two-sided ideal, which licenses passing to the quotient as an algebra, and the trace at z = q^3/(q^2+1) is the standard normalised Temperley--Lieb trace at loop parameter \delta = [2]_q.

A convention collision: rows versus columns

The Temperley--Lieb stratification via Wenzl's Schur elements is naturally stated in the conjugate convention: at X = Q^{-N} the surviving blocks are those with \lambda_1 \le N, i.e. at most N columns. This section, and the z = q^3/(q^2+1) Markov trace, state the survivors as at most two rows. Both are correct in their own convention, and transporting a result from one to the other requires transposition.

The trap is that the two conventions label different sets of partitions while carrying equal dimension sums. At n = 3 the row-set is \{(3),(2,1)\} and the column-set is \{(2,1),(1^3)\} — disjoint but for (2,1), both summing to 5; at n = 6 the two sets share nothing at all and both still total C_6 = 132. So the Catalan counts agree under either reading, and a check that looks only at dimensions cannot tell the two apart. Checked numerically at n = 3,4,5.

Both halves of that trap are theorems, at every n: transposition is an explicit bijection between the two families, so they are equinumerous; the families are nevertheless different sets (witnessed by the single row (3)); and their squared-dimension totals agree. The equality \dim \lambda = \dim \lambda' used above is proved for this family rather than assumed --- it had been asserted here as though standard, and while it is standard for general partitions, nothing in this corpus had it.

The practical consequence: transposition is the only correct transport between the two conventions, and it is not the identity. At the level of the algebra the transport is the involution \theta above: it carries the row-convention radical onto the kernel of the U_i = T_i + 1 quotient map. Matching totals is not evidence that a theorem carries across.

Theorem The trace radical of the Hecke algebra is the Temperley--Lieb kernel, up to the involution \sigma_i \mapsto -\sigma_i^{-1}. Let K be a field of characteristic zero, let q \in K be nonzero and not a root of unity, and let \delta = q + q^{-1}. Let \theta be the algebra involution of H_n(q) with \theta(\sigma_i) = -\sigma_i^{-1} = (q - q^{-1}) - \sigma_i. Then

  \ker \pi \;=\; \theta(\mathrm{rad}),

and H_n(q)/\mathrm{rad} \cong TL_{n+1}(\delta) as K-algebras, with \sigma_i + \mathrm{rad} \mapsto q - e_i. The inclusion \ker \pi \subseteq \mathrm{rad} fails for n = 2.
prop:markov-gram-star-positive:
Proposition The Markov--Gram star form is positive semidefinite; positivity reduces to y_\lambda \ge 0. Let T_w^{*} = T_{w^{-1}} be the Hecke star and let

  S_{ij} \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_M\!\bigl(b_i\,b_j^{*}\bigr)

be the Gram matrix of the Markov trace on the normal-form basis b \in \{\gamma,\, \sigma_0,\, \sigma_1,\, L_+,\, L_-,\, e^{-}\} of H_3(q). Then S is positive semidefinite whenever every Wedderburn weight satisfies y_\lambda \ge 0, and its kernel is spanned by the blocks with y_\lambda = 0.

Positivity is a block computation, not a measurement

Wedderburn decomposes H_3(q) into matrix algebras, one per partition, and the Markov trace acts on the block of \lambda as y_\lambda times the matrix trace. The star form therefore splits as

  \mathrm{tr}_M(a\,a^{*}) \;=\; \sum_{\lambda \vdash 3} y_\lambda \cdot
  \mathrm{tr}\!\bigl(A_\lambda A_\lambda^{*}\bigr),

and on each M_d the sesquilinear trace \mathrm{tr}(AA^{*}) is the sum of the squares of the matrix entries. A nonnegative combination of sums of squares is nonnegative, and it vanishes only when every block with y_\lambda > 0 vanishes. Positivity of the whole form is thus equivalent to nonnegativity of the weights, and the degeneracy locus is exactly the set of blocks the trace kills.

For H_3(q) at the Markov parameter z = q^3/(q^2+1), the weights of (3) and (2,1) are strictly positive for q > 0 while the weight of (1^{3}) vanishes identically, so S acquires a one-dimensional kernel and nothing else: signature (5,0,1).

That kernel is the row cap seen through the pairing. Quotienting by it leaves a genuine inner product, which is what a Rieffel Lipschitz seminorm requires.

The star is what makes the form positive

Positivity is a statement about the star pairing and about no other. The Hecke star sends the basis element of a word to the basis element of its inverse, which on the normal-form basis swaps L_+ \leftrightarrow L_- and fixes the remaining four vectors. That single swap flips the sign of the one antisymmetric direction in the mixed-symmetry block, and the sign it flips is the whole difference between the two pairings. No signature claim about the Markov--Gram form is meaningful until the pairing is named.

rem:markov-gram-bilinear-vs-star:
Remark Two pairings, two signatures: \mathrm{tr}_M(b_ib_j) versus \mathrm{tr}_M(b_ib_j^{*}). The normal-form basis of H_3(q) admits two Gram matrices, and they do not have the same signature. Which one is meant has to be said.

The bilinear pairing

Dropping the star and pairing G_{ij} = \mathrm{tr}_M(b_i b_j) gives, block by block, the bilinear trace form \mathrm{tr}(AB) on each matrix algebra. Parametrise A \in M_2 by its symmetric part (\alpha,\delta,\beta) and its antisymmetric part \gamma, so that

  A \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & \beta+\gamma \\ \beta-\gamma & \delta \end{pmatrix}.

Then

  \mathrm{tr}(A^{2}) \;=\; \alpha^{2} \;+\; 2\beta^{2} \;-\; 2\gamma^{2} \;+\; \delta^{2}.

Three squares enter with a plus sign and one with a minus, and the symmetric and antisymmetric parts are orthogonal, so \mathrm{tr}(AB) on M_d has signature \bigl(\tfrac{d(d+1)}{2},\, \tfrac{d(d-1)}{2}\bigr). Summing over the blocks with y_\lambda > 0 reproduces the whole signature of G: at z = q^3/(q^2+1) on H_3(q), where y_{(1^3)} = 0, the signature is (4,1,1).

The negative direction is identified rather than measured. It is the antisymmetric element E_{12} - E_{21} of the M_2 sitting in the (2,1) block --- the rotation generator of \mathfrak{sl}_2. Any algebra with a two-dimensional irrep contributes one such direction, so G is indefinite for every q and for every convention with y_{(2,1)} > 0. The indefiniteness is a property of the pairing, not of the aether.

An earlier reading took the single negative eigenvalue of G as a physical signature: the trace pairing was said to be a spacetime form, and the framework's natural object a causal structure rather than a metric space. That causal-signature interpretation does not apply: a metric is built from the *-structure, and the Hecke *-structure is T_w^{*} = T_{w^{-1}}. Pairing against it replaces the bilinear \mathrm{tr}(AB) by the sesquilinear \mathrm{tr}(AB^{*}), which on M_d is a sum of d^{2} squares: signature (d^{2},0), no negative direction anywhere. The eigenvalue magnitudes are unchanged --- the star flips exactly the sign of the antisymmetric direction, which is what a *-structure is for --- and the sign flip is what the star form's positivity records.

The bilinear analysis is retained because it is the same block decomposition that explains both answers. It is the interpretation that was wrong, not the arithmetic.

prop:gram-degeneracy-blocks-connes:
Proposition A Lipschitz seminorm with nonzero kernel has no finite Connes sup. Let L be a Lipschitz seminorm on an algebra of observables, let \varphi and \psi be states, and let

  d(\varphi,\psi) \;=\; \sup\,\bigl\{\, |\varphi(a) - \psi(a)| \;:\; L(a) \le 1 \,\bigr\}

be the associated Connes distance. If some k satisfies L(k) = 0 while \varphi(k) \ne \psi(k), then the supremum is unbounded: for every proposed bound M there is an admissible b with |\varphi(b) - \psi(b)| > M.

The argument in one line

Homogeneity and subadditivity give L(a + tk) \le L(a) + |t|\,L(k) = L(a), so the whole line a + tk stays inside the unit ball of the seminorm, while the objective

  \varphi(a+tk) - \psi(a+tk)
  \;=\; \bigl(\varphi(a)-\psi(a)\bigr) \;+\; t\,\bigl(\varphi(k)-\psi(k)\bigr)

grows linearly in t. Choosing t large enough overshoots any bound. The distance is +\infty as posed, not a hard computation.

Stating the conclusion as "no upper bound exists" rather than "d = \infty" keeps the statement inside an ordered field, with no top element adjoined.

Why the framework runs into it

The natural candidate for a derived metric on the state space is the Gram form of the Markov trace: build a Lipschitz seminorm from it, take the Connes supremum, and read off a distance. At the Markov parameter z = q^3/(q^2+1) that route is blocked before it starts. The star form is positive semidefinite with a one-dimensional kernel --- the block killed by the row cap --- and a kernel of the form is a kernel of the seminorm. Any state pair separating that direction supplies the k above.

The obstruction is a fact about the method, and it names its own repair: quotient by the radical, or choose a different seminorm.

cor:finite-connes-forces-trivial-kernel:
Corollary Finite Connes distance forces a trivial kernel --- hence the quotient by the radical. Suppose the Connes supremum is finite: some M bounds |\varphi(b) - \psi(b)| over every b with L(b) \le 1. Then no kernel element of L separates \varphi from \psi --- for every k with L(k) = 0 one has \varphi(k) = \psi(k).

This is the contrapositive of the obstruction, and it is worth stating separately because it converts a negative result into an instruction. Finiteness of the distance is not something one may hope for and then check; it is equivalent to the seminorm having no separating kernel. A construction that wants a finite distance must therefore arrange the kernel away first.

On the Markov--Gram form the arrangement is forced and unique. The kernel is the radical of the pairing, so the only way to satisfy the hypothesis is to pass to the quotient by it. What makes this a restatement rather than an amputation is the identification of the quotient: the radical is the Temperley--Lieb ideal, and H_n(q)/\mathrm{rad} is TL_n(q), an algebra with its own diagrammatic calculus and its own standard form. The instruction "quotient so the distance exists" and the instruction "work in Temperley--Lieb" are the same instruction, and the Catalan count is what identifies them.

On the quotient the star form is positive definite, since the surviving blocks are exactly those with y_\lambda > 0 and each contributes a sum of squares. A definite form is what a Rieffel Lipschitz seminorm needs, so the construction that the degeneracy blocked runs unobstructed one level down.

One qualification travels with the repair. Deleting the radical is observationally free: no trace value moves, because the deleted block already contributed zero.

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha \cdot \sigma_g) \;=\; z \cdot \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha)

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha \cdot \sigma_g^{-1})
  \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha \cdot \sigma_g) - h \cdot \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha)
  \;=\; (z - h) \cdot \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha).

Lemma (block multiplicativity). Let x \in H_{k+1}(q), let y \in H_m(q), and let \mathrm{sh}_{k+1}(y) be y with every \sigma_i replaced by \sigma_{i+k+1}. Then

  \mathrm{tr}_M\bigl(x\,\mathrm{sh}_{k+1}(y)\bigr) = \mathrm{tr}_M(x)\,\mathrm{tr}_M(y),
  \qquad
  \mathrm{tr}_M\bigl(x\,\sigma_k\,\mathrm{sh}_{k+1}(y)\bigr) = z\,\mathrm{tr}_M(x)\,\mathrm{tr}_M(y).

  = z\,\mathrm{tr}_M\bigl(\mathrm{sh}(T_v)\,a\,\mathrm{sh}(T_u)\bigr)

prop:block-multiplicativity-v-free:
Proposition Block-multiplicativity of per-generator \hat{V} on the disjoint Hecke product. Let \mathrm{tr} be a Markov trace with parameter z on the Hecke tower, and let the constituent vacuum \mathcal{B}_K^{\mathrm{vac}} \in H_{3A}(q) be the product of Z proton and N neutron block words on disjoint 3-strand windows (generators 3k, 3k+1 for block k), with no interface crossings. For a generator \sigma_g carrying the accumulated factor W_g = \alpha_g\,\sigma_g + \beta_g, define \hat V_g := \mathrm{tr}(W_g). Then

  \hat V_g \;=\; \beta_g + \alpha_g\, z,

independent of the strand count 3A, of the position g, and of the other blocks. If a block word is the ascending product W_{3k} W_{3k+1}, its trace is \hat V_{3k}\,\hat V_{3k+1}. For any arrangement of the blocks,

  \mathrm{tr}\bigl(\mathcal{B}_K^{\mathrm{vac}}\bigr) \;=\; v_p^{Z}\, v_n^{N},
  \qquad
  v_p = \hat V^{p}_0\, \hat V^{p}_1, \quad v_n = \hat V^{n}_0\, \hat V^{n}_1 .

The proof uses only the trace axioms and the three Hecke relations, over a generic commutative ring. The last identity is the disjoint-block trace law, with each block read at offset 0 by shift invariance.

Scope. The product formula holds for the ascending block word W_{3k}W_{3k+1}. When a block's braid word interleaves its two generators, the trace of that word is \mathrm{tr}(w_p) and not \hat V_0 \hat V_1, because reordering changes the trace. For example, \mathrm{tr}(\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_1\sigma_2) - \mathrm{tr}(\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2) = z^2 - hz - 1 = -(q^4+q^2+1)/(q^2+1)^2 at z = q^3/(q^2+1). The disjoint-block law still gives \mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{B}_K^{\mathrm{vac}}) = \mathrm{tr}(w_p)^Z\,\mathrm{tr}(w_n)^N in that case.
prop:lusztig-vs-hermitian-bar:
Proposition Lusztig bar (q \mapsto q^{-1}) vs Hermitian-\ast (q \mapsto \overline{q}^{-1}) on the complex Hecke algebra: the two anti-involutions coincide on the parameter iff q \in \mathbb{R}. On the unit circle |q| = 1, Lusztig coincides with complex conjugation (\overline{q} = q^{-1}) while Hermitian becomes the identity on q; on general |q| > 1 with \mathrm{Im}(q) \neq 0 the three involutions (Lusztig, Hermitian, complex conjugation) are pairwise distinct. The split is the categorical home for any future \mathrm{Im}(q_0) contribution. On the complex Iwahori–Hecke algebra H_n(\mathbb{C}, q) with q \in \mathbb{C}^\times, the two ring anti-involutions

\beta_L \colon q \mapsto q^{-1},\quad \sigma_i \mapsto \sigma_i^{-1}
\qquad\text{(Lusztig bar)},
\beta_H \colon q \mapsto \overline{q}^{\,-1},\quad \sigma_i \mapsto \sigma_i^{-1}
\qquad\text{(Hermitian \(\ast\))}

coincide on the parameter q if and only if \mathrm{Im}(q) = 0, equivalently q \in \mathbb{R}.

Significance

The framework's existing bar-symmetric / bar-anti-symmetric decomposition is built around \beta_L alone. On the real axis this is the only available involution structure. On general complex q with \lvert q \rvert > 1 and \mathrm{Im}(q) \neq 0, the algebra admits a finer decomposition by simultaneous \beta_L- and \beta_H-eigenvalues, producing four channels:

\beta_L-eigenvalue \beta_H-eigenvalue Existing name Comment
+1 +1 bar-symmetric, Hermitian retained (current)
+1 -1 bar-symmetric, anti-Hermitian new (CP-odd, parity-even?)
-1 +1 bar-anti-symmetric, Hermitian new (CP-even, parity-odd?)
-1 -1 bar-anti-symmetric, anti-Hermitian projected away

The interpretation of the two new channels remains open. This proposition only records the structural existence of the decomposition; it does not claim either new channel corresponds to physical structure.

Non-claims of this proposition (CAL-4 caveat)

  • It does not claim \mathrm{Im}(q_0) \neq 0.
  • It does not claim the two new channels carry physical content.
  • It does not introduce a further calibration input.

It claims only that on complex q with \mathrm{Im}(q) \neq 0 the two anti-involutions split, and that the framework's current real-axis convention makes the split invisible.
prf:lusztig-vs-hermitian-bar:
Proof Proof of lusztig vs hermitian bar. The two involutions act identically on the braid generators \sigma_i (both send \sigma_i \mapsto \sigma_i^{-1}), so the question reduces to the parameter action. Then \beta_L(q) = q^{-1} and \beta_H(q) = \overline{q}^{\,-1}. For q \in \mathbb{C}^\times,

q^{-1} \;=\; \overline{q}^{\,-1} \;\iff\; q \;=\; \overline{q} \;\iff\; \mathrm{Im}(q) = 0. \quad\square

Three cases of complex q

The following table organises the relationship between the three relevant involutions on \mathbb{C}^\times — the Lusztig bar \beta_L, the Hermitian \ast (\beta_H), and complex conjugation \beta_C \colon q \mapsto \overline{q} — as q moves through the three structural regimes:

Regime \beta_L(q) \beta_H(q) \beta_C(q) Equalities
Real axis \mathrm{Im}(q) = 0 q^{-1} q^{-1} q \beta_L = \beta_H; \beta_C = \mathrm{id}
Unit circle \lvert q \rvert = 1 q^{-1} q q^{-1} \beta_L = \beta_C (on parameter); \beta_H = \mathrm{id} on parameter
General \lvert q \rvert > 1, \mathrm{Im}(q) \neq 0 q^{-1} \overline{q}^{\,-1} \overline{q} all three distinct on parameter

The "real-axis" row is the current framework convention. The "unit-circle" row is the regime already discussed in commutative-chirality-vanishes. The "general" row is uncharted; it is the categorical home for any future \mathrm{Im}(q_0) \neq 0 hypothesis.

Decomposition law

The three involutions satisfy

\beta_H \;=\; \beta_C \circ \beta_L \;=\; \beta_L \circ \beta_C

as automorphisms of the coefficient ring \mathbb{C} extended identically over the braid generators. On the real axis \beta_C is the identity, so \beta_H collapses to \beta_L. On the unit circle \beta_C = \beta_L on the parameter (both send q \mapsto q^{-1}), so \beta_H becomes the identity on the parameter. Off both, the three are independent.
prop:q-zero-complex-extension:
Proposition The pre-Archimedean aether is polymorphic in its base ring: specializing to R = \mathbb{C} with |q| > 1 is admissible without modifying the Hecke quadratic, the bar involution, the Frobenius pairing, or the Markov trace. prop:cellular-depth-filtration:
Proposition Cell-depth filtration of Z(H_n(q)): GB-depth as Lusztig's a-function, a filtration by ideals that the Goldman involution carries to the n(\lambda)-filtration; conditional parity transfer. Let K be a field and q\in K^\times such that H_n=H_n(K,q) is split semisimple, let \{e_\lambda\}_{\lambda\vdash n} be its central primitive idempotents, and let Z=Z(H_n). For a function \delta from partitions of n to \mathbb N, the cellular \delta-filtration of Z is

F^\delta_k := \operatorname{span}_K\{e_\lambda : \delta(\lambda)\le k\},\qquad k\in\mathbb N.

The GB-depth of \lambda is Lusztig's a-function of the two-sided Kazhdan–Lusztig cell of shape \lambda, which in the labelling where (n) is the index representation is

a(\lambda)=\sum_i\binom{\lambda_i}{2}.

Write n(\lambda)=\sum_i(i-1)\lambda_i, so that a(\lambda')=n(\lambda). Let \# be the Goldman involution \sigma_i\mapsto-\sigma_i^{-1}, which satisfies \#(e_\lambda)=e_{\lambda'} (Schur-Weyl justification of shell-operator self-duality). Then:

  1. (Filtration by ideals.) For every \delta: F^\delta_j\subseteq F^\delta_k for j\le k; F^\delta_j\cdot F^\delta_k\subseteq F^\delta_{\min(j,k)}, so each F^\delta_k is an ideal of Z; and 1\in F^\delta_k if and only if k\ge\max_\lambda\delta(\lambda). So if \delta>0 somewhere, F^\delta is not a unital algebra filtration.
  2. (Transport by \#.) \#(F^\delta_k)=F^{\delta\circ t}_k, where t(\lambda)=\lambda'. For the GB-depth this reads \#(F^a_k)=F^{n}_k. For n\ge2 the GB-depth filtration is not \#-stable: F^a_0=Ke_{(1^n)} and \#(F^a_0)=Ke_{(n)}. A depth \delta gives a \#-stable filtration if and only if \delta(\lambda')=\delta(\lambda) for all \lambda; examples are the symmetrised depth a(\lambda)+a(\lambda') and the max-hook depth \lambda_1+\lambda'_1-1.
  3. (Eigenvectors.) e_\lambda is \#-fixed if and only if \lambda=\lambda'. For \lambda\ne\lambda', e_\lambda+e_{\lambda'} and e_\lambda-e_{\lambda'} are (+1)- and (-1)-eigenvectors. If \operatorname{char}K\ne2, then Z=Z^+\oplus Z^- with \dim Z^\pm=\tfrac12\bigl(p(n)\pm sc(n)\bigr), where sc(n) is the number of self-conjugate partitions of n. (This dimension count follows directly by counting the +1 and -1 eigenvectors listed above.)
  4. (Conditional parity transfer.) Let P be a K-vector space with a linear involution \iota and projections \pi_d, let \Phi:Z\to P be linear, and assume \operatorname{char}K\ne2 together with the hypotheses (H-match) \Phi\circ\#=\iota\circ\Phi and (H-parity) \pi_d\circ\iota=(-1)^d\pi_d. Then \pi_d\Phi(e_\lambda)=0 for odd d when \lambda=\lambda'; \pi_d\Phi(e_{\lambda'})=(-1)^d\pi_d\Phi(e_\lambda) for all \lambda; and for odd d, \pi_d\Phi(e_\lambda)\ne0 if and only if \pi_d\Phi(e_\lambda)\ne\pi_d\Phi(e_{\lambda'}).

Item 4 does not depend on the depth filtration at all: it is a statement about the idempotents e_\lambda. Neither (H-match) nor (H-parity) is established in the corpus. Item 2 shows that the GB-depth filtration and the transposition \lambda\mapsto\lambda' are not compatible, so the parity picture cannot be phrased as "\# preserves GB-depth".

The statistic \lambda_1+\lambda'_1-1 (the maximal hook length of \lambda) is referred to here as the max-hook depth, distinguishing it from Lusztig's a-function a(\lambda).
prf:cellular-depth-filtration:
Proof Proof of the cell-depth filtration properties. The a-function value. That the two-sided cell of shape \lambda has a-value \sum_i\binom{\lambda_i}2 (with (n) the index representation) is the type-A case of Lusztig's a-function, with each two-sided cell carrying exactly one irreducible [Kazhdan–Lusztig 1979]. It was checked exactly for n\le5 by computing the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis, the cells and a from the structure constants (probe recorded on issue #8094). Writing \binom{\lambda_i}{2}=0+1+\dots+(\lambda_i-1), a(\lambda) is the sum over cells (i,j) of \lambda of the column index j, and n(\lambda) is the sum of the row index i. Transposition swaps i and j, so a(\lambda')=n(\lambda).

Item 1. The e_\lambda are orthogonal idempotents, e_\lambda e_\mu=\delta_{\lambda\mu}e_\lambda, so a product of two generators of F_j and F_k is either 0 or a generator e_\lambda with \delta(\lambda)\le\min(j,k). Bilinearity gives F_jF_k\subseteq F_{\min(j,k)}. If 1\in F_k and \delta(\mu)>k, then e_\mu annihilates every generator of F_k, hence e_\mu=e_\mu\cdot1=0, a contradiction; conversely 1=\sum_\lambda e_\lambda.

Item 2. \# is an algebra automorphism sending each generator e_\lambda of F^\delta_k to e_{\lambda'}, and \delta(\lambda)=(\delta\circ t)(\lambda')\le k. So \#(F^\delta_k)\subseteq F^{\delta\circ t}_k, and applying \# again (it is an involution and t\circ t=\mathrm{id}) gives equality. With \delta=a, a\circ t=n. For n\ge2, the only partition with a(\lambda)=0 is (1^n) and \#(e_{(1^n)})=e_{(n)} with a((n))=\binom n2>0. Stability holds if and only if every level set of \delta is closed under t, which is \delta\circ t=\delta. The max-hook depth is transpose-invariant because the hook of (i,j) in \lambda' equals the hook of (j,i) in \lambda.

Item 3. Orthogonal nonzero idempotents are distinct, so e_{\lambda'}=e_\lambda if and only if \lambda'=\lambda. The eigenvector statements follow from \#(e_\lambda)=e_{\lambda'} and \#^2=\mathrm{id}. The dimension count uses linear algebra on the basis \{e_\lambda\}.

Item 4. (a) For \lambda=\lambda', \iota\Phi(e_\lambda)=\Phi(\#e_\lambda)=\Phi(e_\lambda), so for odd d, \pi_d\Phi(e_\lambda)=\pi_d\iota\Phi(e_\lambda)=-\pi_d\Phi(e_\lambda), which is 0 since 2 is invertible. (b) \pi_d\Phi(e_{\lambda'})=\pi_d\iota\Phi(e_\lambda)=(-1)^d\pi_d\Phi(e_\lambda). (c) For odd d and x=\pi_d\Phi(e_\lambda), (b) gives \pi_d\Phi(e_{\lambda'})=-x, and x\ne-x if and only if x\ne0.

The identity \#(e_\lambda)=e_{\lambda'} used in items 2–4 is taken from [Mathas 1999, Ch. 3] and [Dipper–James 1986]; given it, items 1–4 hold for any commutative algebra Z with orthogonal idempotents e:\iota\to Z. \blacksquare
def:hecke-curvature-2-cocycle:
Definition Hecke curvature 2-cocycle F. The Hecke curvature 2-cocycle is the 2-form-valued bilinear map F \in C^2(H_n(R, q), H_n(R, q)) defined on generator pairs by the deviation from Hecke and Yang-Baxter flat relations:

  F(\sigma_i, \sigma_j) \;=\;
  \begin{cases}
    R_H(i) & \text{if } i = j, \\
    R_{YB}(i) & \text{if } |i - j| = 1, \\
    [\sigma_i, \sigma_j] & \text{if } |i - j| \geq 2.
  \end{cases}

It extends to general elements via the Leibniz rule.
